language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈaɪ̯nəm koˈleːɡən]; in casual speech einem may reduce to [nəm]. Kollegen has stress on long close-mid [eː].
language_specific.usage: The reduced article is optional in speech; the written form remains einem.

common.sentence: Hat er den Stecker geprüft, bevor wir einschalten?

language_specific.grammar: Hat is the third-person singular perfect auxiliary; er is the subject and geprüft the participle.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [hat ʔeːɐ̯], with short [a] and long close-mid [eː]. Unstressed er can join the verb as [ɐ], giving [ˈhatɐ] without a separate glottal onset.
language_specific.usage: The joined pronunciation is optional in speech; standard writing retains Hat er.

common.sentence: Geht es bei deinem Einwand um die Kosten?
common.meaning: finite component of es geht um etwas: does it concern

language_specific.grammar: In es geht um etwas, es is the impersonal subject and um governs the accusative topic.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ɡeːt ʔɛs], with long close-mid [eː] and short open-mid [ɛ]. In rapid speech unstressed es can reduce to [s], yielding [ɡeːts].
language_specific.usage: The reduction is optional in speech; standard writing retains Geht es.

common.sentence: Im Bericht steht, sie lache trotz der schwierigen Lage.

language_specific.grammar: Lache is third-person singular Konjunktiv I; the indicative is lacht.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈlaxə]: stressed [a] is short, followed by [x] and final schwa. The ending distinguishes this form from indicative lacht [laxt]; it should be retained when making that distinction.
language_specific.recognition: Reported-speech recognition: the report attributes the claim that she laughs to its source.

common.sentence: Gib mir bitte ein Zeichen, sobald die Verbindung wieder steht.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of gib; mir identifies the recipient.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ʔaɪ̯n ˈt͡saɪ̯çən]; an unstressed ein can reduce to [ən] in casual speech. Zeichen begins with [t͡s] and has stressed [aɪ̯].
language_specific.usage: The reduction is optional in speech; standard writing retains ein.

common.sentence: Beim Test öffnet der Automat die Klappe erst nach dem Signal.

language_specific.grammar: Öffnet is third-person singular present; die Klappe is its accusative object.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈʔœfnət]: stressed [œ] is short and rounded. The ending contains schwa before [t], supporting the consonant sequence after the stem.
language_specific.usage: The written ending remains -et; casual speech does not make every schwa freely deletable.

common.sentence: Nach einer Weile war die Ursache des Fehlers klar.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after temporal nach.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈaɪ̯nɐ ˈvaɪ̯lə]; in relaxed speech the unstressed article may be [nɐ]. Weile has stressed [aɪ̯] and final schwa.
language_specific.usage: The reduced article is optional in speech; standard writing remains einer.

common.sentence: Ich gebe dir einen Stift, falls deiner nicht mehr schreibt.

language_specific.grammar: Gebe is first-person singular present; dir is the dative recipient and einen Stift the accusative object.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈɡeːbə diːɐ̯]; casual [ɡeːp dɐ] is possible when the final schwa is omitted and dir is unstressed. The verb vowel remains long close-mid [eː].
language_specific.usage: The compressed pronunciation is optional; standard writing retains gebe dir.

common.sentence: Ich sage dir gleich, welcher Schlüssel zur hinteren Tür passt.

language_specific.grammar: Sage is first-person singular present; dir is the dative recipient of the information.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈzaːɡə diːɐ̯]; casual speech can omit the final schwa and weaken dir, yielding [zaːk dɐ]. The verb vowel is long [aː].
language_specific.usage: The compressed pronunciation is optional; standard writing retains sage dir.

common.sentence: Ich glaube, wir sollten erst den Strom ausschalten.

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present; the following clause gives the speaker's opinion.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈɡlaʊ̯bə]; casual [ɡlaʊ̯p] can result from omission of final schwa and final devoicing. The stem contains [aʊ̯].
language_specific.usage: The reduced pronunciation is optional in conversation; the standard written form is glaube.

common.sentence: In Österreich sagte eine Besucherin „Chirurgie“ und meinte die Fachabteilung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted word is the accusative object of sagte; die Fachabteilung identifies the hospital-department sense.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Chirurgie: de-DE [çiʁʊʁˈɡiː]; an Austrian variant is [kiʁʊʁˈɡiː]. The initial consonants differ; [ʊ] is short and lax, and the final stressed [iː] is long and close.
language_specific.recognition: Regional accent recognition: initial [k] is especially associated with Austria, but is not universal there. The neutral de-DE model given here begins with [ç]; the written form remains Chirurgie.

common.sentence: Ich halte die Leiter, während du die Lampe befestigst.

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present; die Leiter is the accusative object.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈhaltə]; casual [halt] can omit final schwa. The stressed [a] is short and the final [t] remains audible.
language_specific.usage: The reduced pronunciation is optional in conversation; standard writing retains halte.

common.sentence: Ich rate dir, zu helfen: Deine Nachbarin braucht Unterstützung.

language_specific.grammar: Dir is the dative recipient of rate; zu helfen states the advised action. The addressee is to help the neighbor.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [diːɐ̯ | t͡suː ˈhɛlfən]: dir and zu have long close vowels; helfen has stressed short open-mid [ɛ]. A boundary after dir supports grouping it with rate. Without that grouping, dir zu helfen can also mean to help you.
language_specific.usage: The clause after the colon identifies the neighbor as the person needing help. The boundary is a possible cue, not proof of the intended interpretation.

common.sentence: Ich finde den Plan gut, aber der Termin ist knapp.

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present; gut describes the accusative object den Plan.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: careful [ˈfɪndə]; casual [fɪnt] can omit final schwa and devoice final d. The stem vowel is short lax [ɪ].
language_specific.usage: The reduced pronunciation is optional in speech; the standard written form is finde.

common.sentence: In der Schweiz nannte ein Besucher die Fachabteilung „Chirurgie“.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted word is an accusative naming complement with nannte; die Fachabteilung is the accusative object being named.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Chirurgie: de-DE [çiʁʊʁˈɡiː]; a Swiss variant is [xiʁʊʁˈɡiː]. The initial consonants differ; [ʊ] is short and lax, and the final stressed [iː] is long and close.
language_specific.recognition: Regional accent recognition: initial [x] is often heard in Switzerland, though not from every speaker. The neutral de-DE model given here begins with [ç]; the written form remains Chirurgie.

common.sentence: Wir haben den Karton eben neben die Tür gestellt.

language_specific.grammar: Neben takes accusative die Tür for the destination of gestellt.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target: [ˈneːbən diː] or [ˈneːbn̩ diː]; the unstressed ending of neben can contain syllabic [n̩]. Its stressed [eː] and the article's full [iː] are long.
language_specific.usage: Close grouping and syllabic [n̩] are optional in speech; standard spelling remains neben die.

common.sentence: Am Spielende applaudierten die Zuschauer beiden Mannschaften noch lange.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after am, the contraction of an dem; the phrase specifies when the applause occurred.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈʃpiːlˌʔɛndə]: Spiel has long close [iː]; Ende begins with short open-mid [ɛ] and can have a glottal onset at the compound boundary. Compare bare plural nominalized participle Spielende [ˈʃpiːləndə], people playing: the ending follows the stem without that compound juncture.
language_specific.usage: The article and time expression identify the end of the game; spelling alone does not convey every spoken boundary cue.

common.sentence: Das Labor untersucht die Probe und meldet sich morgen.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of untersucht and meldet sich.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [laˈboːɐ̯]: stress falls on the second syllable, with long close-mid [oː] followed by vocalized r; the first vowel is unstressed.

common.sentence: Sie beobachtet den Mann mit dem Fernglas; sie benutzt es selbst.

language_specific.grammar: Mit governs dative dem Fernglas. Here the phrase gives the instrument of beobachtet; es refers to the binoculars.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [mɪt deːm ˈfɛʁnˌɡlaːs]: mit has short lax [ɪ], dem long close-mid [eː], and Fernglas stressed short open-mid [ɛ] and long [aː]. A boundary after Mann can support grouping the phrase with the act of observing.
language_specific.usage: The continuation identifies the observer as the user of the binoculars. Without it, the phrase could instead describe the man; a boundary alone need not settle the interpretation.

common.sentence: Mira meinte die rote Mappe, nicht den roten Ordner.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of meinte; rote has weak -e after die.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈʁoːtə ˈmapə]: rote has long close-mid [oː], while Mappe has short [a]. The main contrastive accent can fall on Mappe, since the color is shared.
language_specific.usage: The contrast identifies the kind of item, not its color.

common.sentence: Lena wollte den kleinen Karton, nicht den großen Karton.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of wollte; kleinen has weak -en after den.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈklaɪ̯nən kaʁˈtɔŋ]: kleinen has stressed [aɪ̯]; this pronunciation of Karton has final stress on short open-mid [ɔ] followed by [ŋ]. The contrastive accent can fall on kleinen.
language_specific.usage: The contrast concerns size; both alternatives are boxes.

common.sentence: Du sollst die Datei öffnen, nicht sofort bearbeiten.

language_specific.grammar: Datei is accusative singular after die; öffnen is an infinitive governed by sollst.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [daˈtaɪ̯ ˈʔœfnən]: Datei has final stress on [aɪ̯]; öffnen begins with short rounded [œ]. The contrastive accent can fall on öffnen.
language_specific.usage: The contrast specifies the action requested, while the same file remains the object.

common.sentence: Die Liste liegt noch hier; abgegeben wird sie erst morgen.

language_specific.grammar: Erst limits the time expression morgen; the passive clause places abgegeben first.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ʔeːɐ̯st ˈmɔʁɡn̩]: erst has long close-mid [eː] and vocalized r; morgen has short open-mid [ɔ]. Morgen can carry the main accent.
language_specific.usage: The accent highlights the future submission time against the visible present location.

common.sentence: Ich habe nur den Anfang gelesen; der Schluss fehlt mir noch.

language_specific.grammar: Den Anfang is the accusative object of gelesen; nur restricts the part read.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [nuːɐ̯ deːn ˈʔanfaŋ]: nur and den have long vowels; Anfang has short stressed [a]. Anfang can carry the focus accent.
language_specific.usage: The visible reference to the unread ending supports the restricted reading.

common.sentence: Wir gehen nicht wegen des Lärms, sondern wegen des Rauchs.

language_specific.grammar: Wegen governs genitive des Lärms. Nicht rejects the stated reason; sondern introduces the actual reason.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [nɪçt ˈveːɡən dɛs ˈlɛʁms]: nicht has short lax [ɪ], wegen long close-mid [eː], and Lärms short open-mid [ɛ]. Lärms can receive contrastive prominence against Rauchs.
language_specific.usage: The continuation establishes that the departure occurs because of smoke. Prosody can highlight the contrast but does not by itself override the syntax.

common.sentence: Mira: Der Kurs entfällt. Ben: Entfällt der Kurs?

language_specific.grammar: Entfällt is the first-position finite verb; der Kurs is its nominative singular subject.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ɛntˈfɛlt deːɐ̯ kʊʁs]: entfällt has stressed short open-mid [ɛ]; Kurs has short lax [ʊ]. A marked rising contour can convey that Ben is echoing the news in surprise; a less marked question contour can simply seek confirmation.
language_specific.usage: Mira's preceding statement supplies the reason for Ben to repeat the information. The written question does not determine his actual tone.

common.sentence: Was Jana gestern erklärte, müssen wir heute gemeinsam überprüfen.

language_specific.grammar: The free relative clause is the fronted object of überprüfen; erklärte is its clause-final preterite verb.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [vas ˈjaːna ˈɡɛstɐn ʔɛɐ̯ˈklɛːɐ̯tə]: Jana has long [aː], gestern short [ɛ], and erklärte stressed long [ɛː]. A phrase boundary may follow erklärte.
language_specific.usage: The boundary groups the fronted content before the main clause; a pause is possible but not obligatory.

common.sentence: Die Pakete, außer dem kleinen, passen alle ins Regal.

language_specific.grammar: Außer governs dative dem kleinen; kleinen stands for the explicitly recoverable Paket and has weak -en.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈʔaʊ̯sɐ deːm ˈklaɪ̯nən]: außer and kleinen contain stressed diphthongs; dem has long close-mid [eː]. The inserted exception can be set off by boundaries on both sides.
language_specific.usage: The phrase excludes the small package from the statement that the packages fit.

common.sentence: Mein Vorschlag, also nur der erste Schritt, betrifft die Verkabelung.

language_specific.grammar: The nominative phrase restates mein Vorschlag; erste has weak -e after der.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [nuːɐ̯ deːɐ̯ ˈʔeːɐ̯stə ʃʁɪt]: erste has long close-mid [eː], Schritt short lax [ɪ]. The explanatory insertion can be grouped between boundaries.
language_specific.usage: The insertion narrows the proposal to an initial step.

common.sentence: Ist das Kabel defekt, oder sitzt der Stecker bloß locker?

language_specific.grammar: Ist is the first-position finite verb; das Kabel is the nominative singular subject and defekt its predicate adjective.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ɪst das ˈkaːbəl deˈfɛkt]: ist has short lax [ɪ], das short [a], Kabel long [aː], and defekt final stress on short open-mid [ɛ]. This complete first alternative may end with rising pitch before oder.
language_specific.usage: The question offers two possible explanations; text alone does not fix the pitch contour.

common.sentence: Geht es um den Preis oder um die Lieferzeit?

language_specific.grammar: Um governs accusative die Lieferzeit in es geht um etwas.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ʊm diː ˈliːfɐˌt͡saɪ̯t]: um has short lax [ʊ], Lieferzeit long close [iː] and [aɪ̯]. The final alternative can end with falling pitch.
language_specific.usage: The listener is asked which of two topics is meant; the written question alone does not certify the contour.

common.sentence: Du hast das Werkzeug eingepackt, oder liegt es noch hier?

language_specific.grammar: Werkzeug is accusative singular after das; eingepackt forms the perfect with hast.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈvɛʁkˌt͡sɔʏ̯k ˈʔaɪ̯nɡəˌpakt]: Werkzeug has short [ɛ] and [ɔʏ̯]; eingepackt has primary stress on [aɪ̯] and short [a] in the stem. A boundary can precede oder.
language_specific.usage: The second clause offers an alternative to the first; the first clause can be spoken with continuing intonation.

common.sentence: Sie kommt heute, glaube ich, erst nach dem Mittagessen.

language_specific.grammar: Glaube is first-person singular present; ich is its subject in the parenthetical clause.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈɡlaʊ̯bə ʔɪç]: glaube has stressed [aʊ̯] and final schwa; ich has short lax [ɪ]. The parenthetical may be spoken with reduced prominence and boundaries around it.
language_specific.usage: The insertion marks the arrival time as the speaker's belief rather than a firm assertion.

common.sentence: Der Termin steht fest, die Uhrzeit allerdings noch nicht.

language_specific.grammar: Uhrzeit is nominative singular; steht fest is understood from the first clause, and noch nicht negates it.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈʔuːɐ̯ˌt͡saɪ̯t ʔalɐˈdɪŋs]: Uhrzeit has long [uː] and [aɪ̯]; allerdings has stress on short lax [ɪ]. Uhrzeit can carry contrastive prominence.
language_specific.usage: The contrast distinguishes the fixed appointment from its still-unsettled time.

common.sentence: Der August tritt nach der Pause mit einer roten Nase auf.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of tritt auf; the red nose supports the clown reading.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target August [ˈaʊ̯ɡʊst]: initial stress on [aʊ̯], followed by short lax [ʊ]. The month August is [aʊ̯ˈɡʊst], with stress on the second syllable.

common.sentence: Im August bleibt die Werkstatt wegen Umbau zwei Wochen geschlossen.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after im, which identifies the month.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target August [aʊ̯ˈɡʊst]: stress falls on short lax [ʊ] in the second syllable; the first has [aʊ̯]. The clown August is [ˈaʊ̯ɡʊst], with initial stress.

common.sentence: Buchhalterisch ist die Ausgabe bereits dem Vorjahr zugeordnet.

language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈbuːxhaltəʁɪʃ]: the Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache recommends initial stress on Buch, with long close [uː]; Halter has short [a]. Noninitial stress is also heard.
language_specific.usage: The adverb limits the statement to how the expense is assigned in the accounts.

common.sentence: Die Chirurgie befindet sich hinter dem zweiten Aufzug.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of befindet sich; Chirurgie refers here to the hospital department.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [çiʁʊʁˈɡiː]: stress falls on the final long close [iː]; the preceding [ʊ] is short and lax. Initial ch is [ç] in this standard pronunciation.

common.sentence: Paul, sagt Mira, kommt später; sie hat ihn angerufen.

language_specific.grammar: Sagt Mira is an inserted reporting clause: Mira is its nominative subject. Paul is the subject of kommt; ihn refers to Paul.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [zaːkt ˈmiːʁa]: sagt has long [aː] and [kt]; Mira has stressed long close [iː]. Boundaries around the insertion group Mira as the speaker, rather than grouping Paul as the subject of sagt.
language_specific.usage: The reporting insertion attributes the claim to Mira; the written comma placement establishes this parse. The phone-call clause says she called Paul but does not independently establish the source of the information. Spoken grouping can make the written attribution easier to follow.

common.sentence: Das Team prüft beide Geräte, aber repariert nur eines.

language_specific.grammar: Eines is the accusative object of repariert and refers to one of the two Geräte.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target nur eines [nuːɐ̯ ˈʔaɪ̯nəs]: nur has long close [uː], and eines begins with the diphthong [aɪ̯]. Eines can carry contrastive prominence.
language_specific.usage: The restriction applies to the number repaired, while both devices are checked.

common.sentence: Die Regie entscheidet nach der Probe über den Schluss.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject; Regie refers here to those directing the production.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Regie [ʁeˈʒiː]: stress falls on the long close [iː]; g represents [ʒ].

common.sentence: Die Einladung gilt auch für Begleitpersonen, nicht allein für Mitglieder.

language_specific.grammar: Für governs accusative plural Begleitpersonen; auch includes them in the invitation.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target auch für Begleitpersonen [aʊ̯x fyːɐ̯ bəˈɡlaɪ̯tpɛʁˌzoːnən]: für has long rounded [yː]; Begleitpersonen can receive the main contrastive prominence.
language_specific.usage: The continuation makes clear that members are included as well.

common.sentence: Den Bericht verschicken wir heute intern, morgen dann extern.

language_specific.grammar: The two adverbs specify the time and audience of verschicken.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target heute intern [ˈhɔʏ̯tə ɪnˈtɛʁn]: heute has [ɔʏ̯] and final schwa; intern has stress on short open-mid [ɛ]. Both elements can be prominent in the paired contrast.
language_specific.usage: The sentence pairs today's internal distribution with tomorrow's external distribution.

common.sentence: Der Schaden ist möglicherweise kleiner als zunächst angenommen.

language_specific.grammar: Kleiner is the comparative predicate adjective; als introduces the earlier assumption.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target möglicherweise kleiner [ˈmøːklɪçɐˌvaɪ̯zə ˈklaɪ̯nɐ]: the initial [øː] is long and rounded, and kleiner has [aɪ̯]. Prominence on möglicherweise can emphasize uncertainty.
language_specific.usage: The smaller estimate is presented as a possibility, not an established result.

common.sentence: Die neue Regel betrifft zunächst ausschließlich eingehende Anträge.

language_specific.grammar: Eingehende Anträge is the accusative plural object of betrifft; eingehende has strong plural -e.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target ausschließlich eingehende Anträge [ˈaʊ̯sʃliːslɪç ˈʔaɪ̯nɡeːəndə ˈʔantʁɛːɡə]: ausschließlich has long close [iː]; prominence on eingehende can highlight which applications are covered.
language_specific.usage: Initially, the rule applies only to incoming applications; the sentence does not specify its later scope.

common.sentence: Die Daten reichen für eine Schätzung, aber nicht für eine Prognose.

language_specific.grammar: Für governs accusative eine Schätzung; the phrase specifies the purpose for which the data suffice.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target für eine Schätzung [fyːɐ̯ ˈʔaɪ̯nə ˈʃɛt͡sʊŋ]: für has long rounded [yː]; Schätzung has short open-mid [ɛ]. Schätzung can be prominent against Prognose.
language_specific.usage: The contrast limits what the data support.

common.sentence: Die Kosten sinken insgesamt, obwohl einzelne Posten teurer werden.

language_specific.pronunciation: Target insgesamt [ɪnsɡəˈzamt]: the first vowel is short lax [ɪ], the final stressed vowel short [a]. Initial stress [ˈɪnsɡəzamt] is also standard; Duden gives initial stress as the Austrian and Swiss norm. Prominence can highlight the overall result.
language_specific.usage: The overall decrease is compatible with increases in individual items.

common.sentence: Wir benötigen die Zahlen getrennt nach Standorten, nicht als Summe.

language_specific.grammar: Nach governs dative plural Standorten; getrennt describes how the figures should be presented.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target getrennt nach Standorten [ɡəˈtʁɛnt naːx ˈʃtantˌʔɔʁtən]: getrennt has short open-mid [ɛ], nach has long [aː], and the compound is stressed on Stand.
language_specific.usage: The requested breakdown contrasts with a single aggregate.

common.sentence: Die Lieferung kommt frühestens Freitag; Donnerstag ist ausgeschlossen.

language_specific.grammar: Freitag is used without an article as a temporal expression; frühestens sets an earliest possible day.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target frühestens Freitag [ˈfʁyːəstn̩s ˈfʁaɪ̯taːk]: frühestens begins with long rounded [yː], while Freitag has [aɪ̯] and long [aː].
language_specific.usage: Friday is a lower limit, not a promise of delivery on that day.

common.sentence: Wir warten im Foyer, bis der Vortrag beginnt.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after im, which contracts in dem and marks location.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Foyer [foaˈjeː]: stress falls on the long close-mid [eː]; the written y corresponds to [j].

common.sentence: Der neue Zugang, also der hinter dem Haus, bleibt nachts offen.

language_specific.grammar: Der refers to masculine Zugang; hinter governs dative dem Haus for location.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target der hinter dem Haus [deːɐ̯ ˈhɪntɐ deːm haʊ̯s]: hinter has short lax [ɪ], Haus has [aʊ̯], and the insertion may be set off by boundaries.
language_specific.usage: The insertion identifies the new entrance; the written commas mark its boundaries.

common.sentence: Mira prüft die Zahlen selbst; die Grafiken überlässt sie Ben.

language_specific.grammar: Die Grafiken is the fronted accusative plural object of überlässt; Ben is the recipient.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target die Grafiken [diː ˈɡʁaːfɪkən]: Grafik has long [aː] and short lax [ɪ]. Grafiken can carry contrastive prominence against Zahlen.
language_specific.usage: The second clause changes the item and identifies Ben as the person handling it.

common.sentence: Laut Eva kommt der Techniker morgen, nicht schon heute.

language_specific.grammar: Laut introduces the named source of the following claim.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target laut Eva [laʊ̯t ˈʔeːva]: laut has [aʊ̯]; Eva begins with long close-mid [eː] and may have a glottal onset. A boundary may follow the attribution.
language_specific.usage: The arrival claim is attributed to Eva; the text alone does not fix the speaker's certainty.

common.sentence: Der Entwurf ist fast fertig; zwei Zahlen fehlen allerdings noch.

language_specific.grammar: Fertig is a predicate adjective; fast modifies its degree.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target fast fertig [fast ˈfɛʁtɪç]: fast has short [a], and fertig has short open-mid [ɛ] and final [ɪç]. Fast may be prominent to emphasize the qualification.
language_specific.usage: The continuation explains why the draft is almost, but not completely, finished.

common.sentence: Die Reparatur dauert höchstens zwei Stunden, vielleicht aber weniger.

language_specific.grammar: Zwei Stunden is an accusative expression of duration; höchstens sets an upper limit.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target höchstens zwei Stunden [ˈhøːçstn̩s t͡svaɪ̯ ˈʃtʊndən]: höchstens has long close-mid rounded [øː], zwei has [aɪ̯], and Stunden has short lax [ʊ].
language_specific.usage: The duration may be shorter than two hours.

common.sentence: Die Gäste dürfen fotografieren, allerdings ohne Blitz im Museum.

language_specific.grammar: Ohne governs accusative Blitz, used without an article for the photographic equipment or effect.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target ohne Blitz [ˈoːnə blɪt͡s]: ohne has long close-mid [oː] and final schwa; Blitz has short lax [ɪ]. A speaker can emphasize the restriction.
language_specific.usage: Photography is permitted subject to the stated restriction.

common.sentence: Zumindest für heute bleibt der Zugang frei, über morgen entscheidet das Team.

language_specific.grammar: The fronted phrase limits the period explicitly covered by the statement; bleibt follows in second position.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target zumindest für heute [t͡suˈmɪndəst fyːɐ̯ ˈhɔʏ̯tə]: zumindest has short lax [ɪ], für has long rounded [yː], and heute has [ɔʏ̯]. A boundary may follow heute.
language_specific.usage: The sentence confirms access today while leaving tomorrow open.

common.sentence: Die Meldung stammt offenbar vom Empfang, nicht von der Leitung.

language_specific.grammar: Vom contracts von dem and governs dative Empfang, the stated source.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target offenbar vom Empfang [ˈʔɔfn̩baːɐ̯ fɔm ɛmˈpfaŋ]: offenbar starts with short open-mid [ɔ], and Empfang has stress on short [a].
language_specific.usage: Offenbar presents the source as an apparent inference; the contrast rules out the management as the stated alternative.

common.sentence: Die Sitzung endet pünktlich; Fragen sammeln wir anschließend schriftlich.

language_specific.grammar: Anschließend specifies when and schriftlich specifies how the questions are collected.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target anschließend schriftlich [ˈʔanʃliːsənt ˈʃʁɪftlɪç]: anschließend has long close [iː]; schriftlich has short lax [ɪ]. Separate prominence can clarify time and manner.
language_specific.usage: The questions are collected after the meeting and in written form.

common.sentence: Das Exposé beschreibt die Idee, aber noch nicht die Umsetzung.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of beschreibt.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Exposé [ɛkspoˈzeː]: stress falls on the long close-mid [eː]; s is voiced [z].

common.sentence: Soll ich den Entwurf schon an die Gruppe weiterleiten?

language_specific.grammar: Soll precedes its subject ich and governs weiterleiten. With a dependent infinitive, the perfect normally uses the replacement infinitive sollen.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Soll ich: careful [zɔl ʔɪç], with short open-mid [ɔ] and short lax [ɪ]. In connected speech the glottal onset may be absent and the words closely grouped.
language_specific.usage: The speaker asks whether forwarding is wanted; the written question does not determine the exact pitch contour.

common.sentence: Möchtest du zuerst die Kosten oder den Zeitplan besprechen?

language_specific.grammar: Möchtest is a subjunctive form of mögen; du is its subject and besprechen the dependent infinitive. With a dependent infinitive, the perfect normally uses the replacement infinitive mögen.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Möchtest du: careful [ˈmœçtəst duː], with short rounded [œ] and long [uː]. In casual connected speech the unstressed pronoun can be shortened and joined closely to the verb.
language_specific.usage: Du marks informal address; the speaker offers a choice of discussion order.

common.sentence: Wir schicken ihm die Skizze jetzt und den Plan später.

language_specific.grammar: Ihm is the dative recipient; die Skizze is the accusative object of schicken.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target ihm die Skizze [iːm diː ˈskɪt͡sə]: ihm and die have long close [iː]; Skizze has short lax [ɪ] and final schwa. Unstressed ihm may be shortened in connected speech.
language_specific.usage: The pronoun's weakening is optional; the recipient remains recoverable from the surrounding conversation.

common.sentence: Gibst du ihr den Schlüssel oder legst du ihn hierhin?

language_specific.grammar: Du is the nominative subject of gibst; ihr is the dative recipient.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target du ihr: careful [duː ʔiːɐ̯], with long close [uː] and [iː]. In connected speech the vowels can be shorter and the boundary less prominent; the pronouns remain distinct words.
language_specific.usage: The question contrasts giving the key to her with putting it here.

common.sentence: Nach dem Konzert erzählen wir Freunden von unserem Rendezvous.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after von; unserem marks the neuter dative.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Rendezvous [ʁɑ̃deˈvuː]: the first vowel is nasalized and back; stress falls on long close [uː]. The standard alternative [ˈʁɑ̃ːdevu] has initial stress and a long nasal vowel. The final written s is silent in these singular forms.
language_specific.usage: In this dated, usually playful use, Rendezvous refers to a romantic meeting; here it is the speakers' date.

common.sentence: Ist denn die zweite Fassung schon bei der Druckerei?
common.meaning: the second version; denn connects the question to the discussion

language_specific.grammar: Die zweite Fassung is the nominative subject of ist; zweite has weak -e after die.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target denn die zweite Fassung [dɛn diː ˈt͡svaɪ̯tə ˈfasʊŋ]: denn has short open-mid [ɛ], zweite has [aɪ̯], and Fassung has short [a]. Unstressed denn can be weakened.
language_specific.usage: Denn connects the question to an ongoing discussion; tone and context determine its precise interpersonal effect.

common.sentence: Ich kann Ihnen den Link schicken, sobald ich wieder online bin.

language_specific.grammar: Kann governs schicken; Ihnen is the dative recipient. With a dependent infinitive, the perfect normally uses the replacement infinitive können.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target kann Ihnen [kan ˈʔiːnən]: kann has short [a], and Ihnen has long close [iː]. In connected speech the glottal onset can be absent without changing the written words.
language_specific.usage: Ihnen addresses the recipient formally; the sentence offers to send the link when the speaker is online again.

common.sentence: Das Paket ist angekommen, aber noch nicht ausgepackt.

language_specific.grammar: Ausgepackt is a participial predicate in an elliptical state-passive clause; a form of sein is understood: das Paket ist noch nicht ausgepackt.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target noch nicht ausgepackt [nɔx nɪçt ˈʔaʊ̯sɡəˌpakt]: noch has short open-mid [ɔ], nicht has short lax [ɪ], and the participle is stressed on aus.
language_specific.usage: The contrast distinguishes arrival from the still-incomplete unpacking.

common.sentence: Wir brauchen vor allem die erste Seite, der Rest kann warten.

language_specific.grammar: Die erste Seite is the accusative object of brauchen; erste has weak -e after die.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target vor allem die erste Seite [foːɐ̯ ˈʔaləm diː ˈʔeːɐ̯stə ˈzaɪ̯tə]: allem has short [a], erste has long close-mid [eː], and Seite has [aɪ̯].
language_specific.usage: The phrase gives the first page priority without excluding the rest.

common.sentence: Ben hat das Glas fast fallen lassen, aber rechtzeitig zugegriffen.

language_specific.grammar: The perfect uses the replacement infinitive lassen with fallen. Fallen has fällt, fiel, gefallen, takes sein in its intransitive perfect, and is inseparable.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target fast fallen lassen [fast ˈfalən ˈlasən]: all three stressed vowels are short [a]; fast may be prominent to signal that the dropping nearly happened.
language_specific.usage: The continuation supports the reading that Ben caught the glass in time.

common.sentence: Nur bei Regen findet das Treffen im Gemeindehaus statt.

noun.plural: no plural in this weather sense

language_specific.grammar: Bei governs dative Regen; the fronted phrase states the exclusive condition for the indoor venue.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target nur bei Regen [nuːɐ̯ baɪ̯ ˈʁeːɡən]: nur has long close [uː], bei has [aɪ̯], and Regen has long close-mid [eː].
language_specific.usage: The restriction concerns the condition for meeting indoors; it does not state the alternative venue.

common.sentence: Der Vorschlag betrifft zunächst die Planung; über die Kosten reden wir später.

language_specific.grammar: Über governs accusative plural die Kosten as the topic of reden.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target über die Kosten [ˈyːbɐ diː ˈkɔstn̩]: über has long close rounded [yː], and Kosten has short open-mid [ɔ]. A boundary can precede the new topic.
language_specific.usage: The second clause shifts the discussion from planning to costs and places it later.

common.sentence: Das Formular ist vollständig, bis auf die fehlende Unterschrift.

language_specific.grammar: Bis auf governs accusative die fehlende Unterschrift; fehlende has weak -e after die.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target bis auf die fehlende Unterschrift [bɪs aʊ̯f diː ˈfeːləndə ˈʊntɐʃʁɪft]: fehlende has long close-mid [eː]; Unterschrift begins with stressed short lax [ʊ].
language_specific.usage: The phrase identifies an exception to the claim of completeness.

common.sentence: Die Abteilung braucht mehr Personal, jedenfalls während der Messe.
common.meaning: at least during the trade fair

language_specific.grammar: Während governs genitive der Messe; the phrase identifies the period for which the claim is maintained.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target jedenfalls während der Messe [ˈjeːdn̩ˌfals ˈvɛːʁənt deːɐ̯ ˈmɛsə]: jedenfalls begins with long close-mid [eː]; Messe has short open-mid [ɛ].
language_specific.usage: The afterthought limits the speaker's firm claim to the fair period.

common.sentence: Das Ballett beginnt erst, wenn alle Gäste sitzen.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of beginnt.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Ballett [baˈlɛt]: stress falls on the second syllable, whose open-mid [ɛ] is short.

common.sentence: Dieses Souvenir erinnert mich an unseren gemeinsamen Urlaub am Meer.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of erinnert; an governs accusative unseren gemeinsamen Urlaub.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Souvenir [zuvəˈniːɐ̯]: initial s is voiced [z]; stress falls on long close [iː], followed by vocalized r.

common.sentence: Das Bouquet des Weins erinnert mich an reife Birnen.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of erinnert; des Weins identifies the wine. The standard Germanized form Bukett is also neuter; its plurals are Buketts and Bukette.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Bouquet [buˈkeː]: stress falls on long close-mid [eː]; qu represents [k], and final t is silent. The accepted Germanized form Bukett is [buˈkɛt], with short open-mid [ɛ] and pronounced final [t].

common.sentence: In dieser Branche ändern sich die technischen Anforderungen besonders schnell.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after in, identifying the sector in which the changes occur.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Branche [ˈbʁaŋʃə]: stressed [a] is short, ch represents [ʃ], and final e is schwa. Also standard is [ˈbʁɑ̃ːʃə], with a long back nasal vowel. Duden additionally records Austrian [bʁɑ̃ːʃ], without final schwa.

common.sentence: Die Choreografie verlangt dem Ensemble viel Geduld bei den Proben ab.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject; dem Ensemble is the dative complement of abverlangen. The accepted spelling Choreographie has plural Choreographien.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Choreografie [koʁeoɡʁaˈfiː]: initial ch is [k], and stress falls on the final long close [iː].

common.sentence: Das Feuilleton bespricht heute den neuen Roman der Autorin.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of bespricht.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Feuilleton [fœjəˈtɔ̃ː]: stress falls on the long nasal final vowel; the first rounded vowel is short and open-mid. Also standard is initial-stressed [ˈfœjətɔ̃], with a short final nasal vowel.

common.sentence: Ihr Ressort betreut die kulturellen Themen der Zeitung.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of betreut.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Ressort [ʁɛˈsoːɐ̯]: the initial [ɛ] is short and open-mid; the stressed [oː] is long and close-mid, followed by vocalized r. The final written t is silent.

common.sentence: Nach der Debatte zieht Mira ein kurzes Resümee.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of zieht in ein Resümee ziehen.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Resümee [ʁezyˈmeː]: stress falls on the long close-mid final vowel; the preceding rounded [y] is unstressed.

common.sentence: Die Silhouette des Turms verschwindet langsam im Nebel.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of verschwindet; des Turms identifies the silhouette.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Silhouette [ziluˈɛtə]: stress falls on short open-mid [ɛ]; the final syllable contains schwa.

common.sentence: Das Plädoyer der Anwältin dauerte fast eine Stunde.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of dauerte; der Anwältin identifies the speaker.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Plädoyer [plɛdoaˈjeː]: stress falls on the long close-mid final vowel; the initial [ɛ] is short and open-mid.

common.sentence: Die Recherche führte das Team zu einem unbekannten Archiv.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of führte.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Recherche [ʁəˈʃɛʁʃə]: stress falls on short open-mid [ɛ]; both unstressed syllables contain schwa.

common.sentence: Ihr Renommee als Forscherin beruht auf sorgfältiger Arbeit.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of beruht; als Forscherin specifies the field of reputation. The plural Renommees is rare.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Renommee [ʁenɔˈmeː]: stress falls on long close-mid [eː]; the preceding [ɔ] is short and open-mid.

common.sentence: Das Gremium berät morgen über die eingegangenen Vorschläge.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of berät.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Gremium [ˈɡʁeːmi̯ʊm]: stress falls on long close-mid [eː]; the ending contains a glide and short [ʊ].

common.sentence: Der Protagonist erkennt seinen Irrtum erst ganz am Schluss.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of erkennt; the weak noun takes -en in the other singular cases.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Protagonist [pʁotaɡoˈnɪst]: final stress falls on short lax [ɪ]; the preceding vowels are unstressed.

common.sentence: Das Intermezzo lockerte die ernste Diskussion für einen Augenblick auf.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of lockerte auf.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Intermezzo [ɪntɐˈmɛtso]: stress falls on short open-mid [ɛ], followed by [ts]; the last vowel is unstressed.

common.sentence: Das Timbre ihrer Stimme verändert sich im Laufe des Liedes.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of verändert sich; ihrer Stimme identifies the voice.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Timbre [ˈtɛ̃ːbʁə]: stress falls on the long nasal open-mid vowel; the final syllable has schwa.

common.sentence: Die Peripherie der Stadt ist nur selten Thema der Reportage.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject; der Stadt specifies the area whose outskirts are meant.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Peripherie [peʁifeˈʁiː]: stress falls on the long close final [iː]; the preceding vowels are unstressed.

common.sentence: Sein Fauxpas beim Empfang sorgte kurz für betretenes Schweigen.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of sorgte; beim Empfang gives the occasion.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Fauxpas [foˈpaː]: stress falls on long [aː]; the first vowel is close-mid, and the written final s is silent.

common.sentence: Das Portfolio zeigt Arbeiten aus verschiedenen Phasen ihres Studiums.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of zeigt.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Portfolio [pɔʁtˈfoːli̯o]: stress falls on long close-mid [oː]; the initial [ɔ] is short and open-mid.

common.sentence: Ihr Metier ist die Gestaltung kleiner Bühnenräume.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of ist; die Gestaltung identifies her field. The accepted spelling Métier has plural Métiers.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Metier [meˈti̯eː]: final stress falls on long close-mid [eː], preceded by a glide.

common.sentence: Die Revanche gelang ihr erst beim nächsten Turnier.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of gelang; ihr names the person who succeeded.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Revanche [ʁəˈvãːʃə]: stress falls on the long nasal vowel; the first and last syllables have schwa.

common.sentence: Der Eklat beendete die Verhandlungen noch vor der Mittagspause.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of beendete.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Eklat [eˈklaː]: stress falls on long [aː]; the initial vowel is unstressed and the final t is silent.

common.sentence: Die Vinaigrette enthält Senf, Essig und etwas Öl.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of enthält.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Vinaigrette [vinɛˈɡʁɛtə]: stress falls on short open-mid [ɛ]; the last syllable contains schwa.

common.sentence: Das Raffinement der Lösung zeigt sich erst bei genauer Betrachtung.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of zeigt sich; der Lösung specifies what has the quality.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Raffinement [ʁafinəˈmɑ̃ː]: stress falls on the long back nasal final vowel; the preceding syllable has schwa.

common.sentence: Das Œuvre der Malerin umfasst auch zahlreiche Zeichnungen.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of umfasst; der Malerin identifies the artist. The accepted Oeuvre spelling has plural Oeuvres.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target Œuvre [ˈœːvʁə] or [ˈøːvʁə]: the stressed rounded vowel is long, with either open-mid or close-mid quality. The final syllable has schwa. Both apply to accepted spelling Oeuvre.

common.sentence: In Österreich bezeichnet „Schmäh“ hier einen humorvollen Einfall.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: Here the word refers to a humorous remark; its precise effect depends on context.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Schmäh has several senses in Austrian usage. A suitable de-DE equivalent here is witziger Einfall.

common.sentence: Im Wiener Gespräch meint „grantig“ eine mürrische Stimmung.

language_specific.usage: The colloquial adjective describes an irritable or grumpy disposition.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: grantig is common in Austria and also used in southern Germany; mürrisch is a broadly usable de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: In Österreich kann „Sudern“ das anhaltende Klagen bezeichnen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominalized infinitive is the subject of kann bezeichnen.
language_specific.usage: The informal word presents the complaining as tiresome or persistent.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Sudern is used in Austrian colloquial speech; ständiges Klagen is a de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im Wiener Gespräch heißt „leiwand“ hier besonders gut.

language_specific.usage: The informal adjective expresses a positive assessment among familiar speakers.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: leiwand is associated especially with Viennese colloquial speech; toll is a broadly usable informal de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Dienstrecht bezeichnet „Vorrückung“ den Aufstieg in eine höhere Gehaltsstufe.
common.meaning: advancement to a higher salary step

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: This sense belongs to formal employment and administrative language.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Vorrückung is an Austrian official term for advancement to a higher salary step. Aufstieg in eine höhere Gehaltsstufe is a suitable de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Personalbericht bezeichnet „Pragmatisierung“ die Ernennung in ein dauerhaftes Beamtenverhältnis.
common.meaning: appointment to a permanent civil-service position

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term belongs to formal personnel and administrative language.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Pragmatisierung is an Austrian official term. Verbeamtung is a related de-DE term; the institutional arrangements differ.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Schreiben bedeutet „allenfalls“ hier gegebenenfalls, nicht höchstens.

language_specific.usage: In Swiss usage, this sense indicates that something applies if circumstances warrant it.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: allenfalls can mean gegebenenfalls in Swiss Standard German. In de-DE, allenfalls often means höchstens or im besten Fall; use gegebenenfalls for the intended sense here.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Schreiben bedeutet „traktieren“ hier jemanden zu einem Essen einzuladen.
common.meaning: treat someone to food or drink

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names a transitive verb; the person treated is its accusative object.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: traktieren can mean to treat someone in Swiss Standard German. In de-DE, jemanden einladen is natural here; traktieren often has a different, negative sense.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht bezeichnet „Konkordat“ eine Vereinbarung zwischen Kantonen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Konkordat can mean an agreement between cantons in Swiss Standard German. Vereinbarung zwischen Kantonen describes this sense in de-DE; Konkordat also has other institutional meanings.

common.sentence: In der Schweizer Korrespondenz bedeutet „verdanken“ hier den Empfang bestätigen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names a transitive verb; the item acknowledged is its accusative object.
language_specific.usage: This formal correspondence sense acknowledges receipt with thanks.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: verdanken can be used in Swiss Standard German correspondence to acknowledge receipt. In de-DE, den Empfang bestätigen is clearer; verdanken commonly means to owe something to someone.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Politikbericht bezeichnet „Konkordanz“ hier das Regieren in einer Koalition.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Konkordanz has a political sense referring to coalition government in Swiss Standard German. Koalitionsregierung is a useful de-DE description; Konkordanz also has other senses.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht leitet der „Landammann“ die Regierung eines Kantons.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of leitet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Landammann is a title for the head of government in certain cantons. Regierungspräsident is a descriptive de-DE comparison; institutional roles differ.

common.sentence: In Norddeutschland kann „klönen“ ein gemütliches Gespräch führen bedeuten.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names an intransitive verb.
language_specific.usage: The informal word suggests relaxed, sociable conversation.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: klönen is associated with northern German speech; sich unterhalten or plaudern is a de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im norddeutschen Gespräch beschreibt „plietsch“ eine aufgeweckte Person.

language_specific.usage: The colloquial adjective praises a person's quick understanding.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: plietsch is a northern regional word; aufgeweckt or klug is a broadly usable de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: In Norddeutschland kann „Schnack“ ein zwangloses Gespräch bedeuten.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of kann bedeuten.
language_specific.usage: The word is informal; here it refers to a sociable conversation.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: Schnack is a regional colloquial word with several senses; Plausch is a de-DE equivalent in this context.

common.sentence: Im Kölner Bericht meint „Klüngel“ hier ein Netz persönlicher Beziehungen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of meint.
language_specific.usage: The word can suggest that personal connections are used to secure favors.
language_specific.recognition: Central and western Germany recognition: Klüngel is associated with the Rhineland, especially Cologne, and is also used more widely. A de-DE description is Netzwerk persönlicher Beziehungen.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Dienstplan bezeichnet „Journaldienst“ einen Bereitschaftsdienst.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term is used in professional duty schedules.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Journaldienst is an Austrian term for Bereitschaftsdienst, a suitable de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Behördenwegweiser nimmt die „Einlaufstelle“ eingehende Post entgegen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of nimmt entgegen; eingehende Post is the accusative object.
language_specific.usage: The term belongs to official administrative language.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Einlaufstelle names an office that receives incoming official mail. Posteingangsstelle is a suitable de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im schwäbischen Gespräch meint „schaffen“ hier beruflich arbeiten.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names the intransitive work sense.
language_specific.recognition: Southern Germany recognition: schaffen can mean arbeiten in Swabian and other southern usage. In de-DE, arbeiten makes this sense clear; schaffen has several other meanings.

common.sentence: In Bayern kann „granteln“ mürrisches Schimpfen oder Klagen bedeuten.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names an intransitive verb.
language_specific.usage: The informal word characterizes the complaining as bad-tempered.
language_specific.recognition: Southern Germany recognition: granteln is associated with Bavaria and Austria; mürrisch schimpfen or meckern is a de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Schreiben bezeichnet „Ansuchen“ einen förmlichen Antrag.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Ansuchen is used in formal Austrian German; Antrag is a common de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Bauverfahren sind „Anrainer“ Grundstücksnachbarn.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative plural is the subject of sind.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Anrainer refers to neighboring residents or property holders; Anlieger is a de-DE equivalent in many contexts.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Protokoll bezeichnet „Einvernahme“ die Befragung einer Person.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term belongs to official and legal language.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Einvernahme is used for official questioning; Vernehmung is a common de-DE equivalent. The term also occurs in Switzerland.

common.sentence: Im Wiener Behördenbrief meint „Erledigung“ hier eine schriftliche behördliche Antwort.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of meint.
language_specific.usage: This is an administrative use of the word for the written handling of a matter.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Erledigung can refer to an official written response; behördliches Schreiben is a useful de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Gerichtsbericht meint „Tagsatzung“ einen angesetzten Gerichtstermin.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of meint.
language_specific.usage: The term belongs to legal procedure.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Tagsatzung is an Austrian legal term; Gerichtstermin is a useful de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Gerichtsverfahren bezeichnet „Exekution“ die zwangsweise Durchsetzung einer Forderung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The legal context selects enforcement proceedings, rather than the word's other senses.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Exekution is used for compulsory enforcement; Zwangsvollstreckung is a related de-DE term, though procedures differ.

common.sentence: Im Wiener Amtsbrief meint „Evidenz“ hier eine geführte Übersicht.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of meint.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Evidenz can refer to an administrative record or list; Übersicht or Verzeichnis can fit in de-DE. In other contexts Evidenz has different senses.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Register bezeichnet „Handänderung“ den Wechsel des Eigentümers eines Grundstücks.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term is used in formal property and financial contexts.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Handänderung is Swiss Standard German for a transfer of ownership; Eigentumsübertragung is a de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Schriftverkehr bezeichnet „Vidierung“ die amtliche Beglaubigung eines Dokuments.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term is formal and occurs in administrative contexts.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Vidierung can denote official certification; Beglaubigung is a useful de-DE equivalent depending on the procedure.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Schreiben bezeichnet „Rechtsvorschlag“ den Einspruch gegen eine Betreibung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term belongs to formal debt enforcement language.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Rechtsvorschlag is a Swiss Standard German procedural term; Einspruch gegen eine Zwangsvollstreckung is an approximate de-DE description, though procedures differ.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Gespräch heißt „eh“ hier sowieso: Der Raum ist schon reserviert.

language_specific.usage: The informal adverb has the contextual meaning sowieso; the sentence says the room is already reserved.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: eh is common in informal Austrian German and also occurs in Germany; ohnehin is a neutral de-DE equivalent here.

common.sentence: Im Wiener Gespräch bedeutet „ur“ vor einem Adjektiv hier besonders.

language_specific.usage: The informal intensifier precedes an adjective, as in ur gut; it is unsuitable for formal correspondence.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: ur is a colloquial intensifier, especially associated with eastern Austria; sehr is a neutral de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: In Österreich bedeutet „ehestmöglich“, dass etwas so bald wie möglich geschieht.

language_specific.usage: The word is used in formal requests and administrative correspondence.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: ehestmöglich is common in Austrian formal German; schnellstmöglich or so bald wie möglich is a de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Schreiben bedeutet „tunlichst“ hier nach Möglichkeit.

language_specific.usage: This formal use qualifies a request by what is practicable; it does not make fulfillment unconditional.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: tunlichst can mean nach Möglichkeit in Austrian formal usage. In Germany it can also convey a strong warning or insistence, depending on context.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Bericht meint „Realitäten“ hier Grundstücke und Gebäude.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted plural is the subject of meint.
language_specific.usage: This property sense is used in business and legal contexts.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Realitäten can mean real estate; Immobilien is a common de-DE equivalent. The general sense realities also exists.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Protokoll bezeichnet „Traktandenliste“ die Liste der Sitzungsthemen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Traktandenliste is Swiss Standard German; Tagesordnung is a common de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Der Schweizer Bericht nennt den kommunalen Amtsinhaber „Gemeindepräsident“.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted noun names the officeholder after nennt; it is a weak noun.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Gemeindepräsident is a Swiss Standard German municipal office title. Bürgermeister is a rough German comparison; responsibilities vary by municipality.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Finanzbeschluss bezeichnet „Verpflichtungskredit“ die Ermächtigung zum Eingehen finanzieller Verpflichtungen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Verpflichtungskredit is a Swiss Standard German public-finance term; Ermächtigung zum Eingehen künftiger finanzieller Verpflichtungen describes it in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bauverfahren bezeichnet „Einsprecher“ eine Person, die Einsprache erhebt.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Einsprecher is a Swiss Standard German procedural term; Person, die Einspruch erhebt is a de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bescheid bezeichnet „Einsprache“ einen formellen Einwand gegen eine Verfügung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term names a formal procedural objection.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Einsprache is used in Swiss Standard German administration; Einspruch or Widerspruch may be appropriate in de-DE, depending on the procedure.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Vertrag bezeichnet „Umtriebsentschädigung“ eine Zahlung für entstandenen Aufwand.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Umtriebsentschädigung is used in Swiss Standard German; Aufwandsentschädigung is a possible de-DE equivalent, depending on the circumstances.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Brief meint „Umtriebe“ hier zusätzlichen Aufwand durch eine Änderung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted plural is the subject of meint.
language_specific.usage: This sense can appear in apologies for inconvenience caused.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Umtriebe can mean inconvenience or extra effort in Swiss Standard German; Unannehmlichkeiten or Mehraufwand may fit in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Schulführer bezeichnet „Fachmittelschule“ einen allgemeinbildenden Ausbildungsgang.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Fachmittelschule names a Swiss upper-secondary school type in Standard German; there is no exact general de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Wahlbericht bezeichnet „Stimmvolk“ die Gesamtheit der Stimmberechtigten.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Stimmvolk is common in Swiss Standard German political reporting; Stimmberechtigte is a useful de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Politikbericht bezeichnet „Volksmehr“ die Mehrheit der gültigen Stimmen für eine Vorlage.
common.meaning: majority of valid votes in favor

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Volksmehr is a Swiss Standard German voting term for a majority of valid votes in favor of a proposal. Mehrheit der gültigen Stimmen für eine Vorlage describes it in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Politikbericht bezeichnet „Ständemehr“ die Mehrheit der Kantonsstimmen für eine Vorlage.
common.meaning: majority of cantonal votes in favor

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Ständemehr is a Swiss Standard German voting term for a majority of cantonal votes in favor of a proposal. Mehrheit der Kantonsstimmen für eine Vorlage describes the institution in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht meint „Abstimmungsbüchlein“ die Erläuterungen zu einer Volksabstimmung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of meint.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Abstimmungsbüchlein is used in Swiss Standard German for an official voting information booklet; Informationsheft zur Abstimmung describes it in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Sitzungsbericht entscheidet bei Stimmengleichheit der „Stichentscheid“ des Vorsitzenden.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of entscheidet; des Vorsitzenden identifies whose casting vote it is.
language_specific.usage: The term is used for a deciding vote when votes are tied.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Stichentscheid is used in Swiss Standard German; ausschlaggebende Stimme is a de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Polizeibericht bezeichnet „Verzeigung“ die Anzeige einer Person bei einer Behörde.
common.meaning: reporting of a person to an authority

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.usage: The term occurs in official and police contexts.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Verzeigung is used in Swiss Standard German; Anzeige is a de-DE equivalent in this context.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Brief bedeutet „allfällig“ hier möglicherweise eintretend.

language_specific.usage: The adjective qualifies something whose occurrence is uncertain, such as allfällige Kosten.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: allfällig is used in Swiss Standard German formal writing; etwaig or möglicherweise entstehend can fit in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im norddeutschen Gespräch kann „tüddelig“ eine zerstreute Person beschreiben.

language_specific.usage: The informal adjective can be affectionate or critical, depending on the relationship and tone.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: tüddelig is a regional colloquial adjective; zerstreut is a neutral de-DE equivalent here.

common.sentence: In Norddeutschland kann „mucksch“ eine beleidigte oder missmutige Stimmung beschreiben.

language_specific.usage: The colloquial adjective describes a person's visible displeasure or sulking.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: mucksch is a regional colloquial adjective; beleidigt or missmutig can fit in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im norddeutschen Gespräch kann „büschen“ eine kleine Menge bedeuten.
common.meaning: little; in the expression ein büschen

language_specific.usage: The word is informal and occurs in phrases such as ein büschen.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: büschen occurs in the regional colloquial expression ein büschen, corresponding to ein bisschen in widespread de-DE.

common.sentence: In Norddeutschland kann „sabbeln“ abwertend für viel Reden stehen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names an intransitive verb.
language_specific.usage: The informal verb can characterize talk as excessive or idle.
language_specific.recognition: Northern Germany recognition: sabbeln is a regional colloquial verb; viel reden or schwatzen can fit in de-DE.

common.sentence: Über die langen Begrüßungsreden sagt die Kollegin abfällig: „Was für ein Gedöns!“

language_specific.grammar: The noun appears in the exclamation was für ein Gedöns.
language_specific.usage: The colloquial exclamation dismisses the speeches as unnecessary fuss.
language_specific.recognition: Ruhr-area recognition: Gedöns is attested in the regional colloquial speech of the Ruhrgebiet and is also used elsewhere. In this dismissive sense, unnötiger Aufwand is a neutral de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im rheinischen Gespräch kann „bützen“ einen Kuss geben bedeuten.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted infinitive names a verb that can take the person kissed as an accusative object.
language_specific.usage: The colloquial word is associated with the Rhineland and carnival customs.
language_specific.recognition: Central western Germany recognition: bützen is a regional colloquial verb; küssen is a neutral de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Im Kölner Karneval bezeichnet „Dreigestirn“ drei gemeinsam auftretende Festfiguren.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Rhineland recognition: the Kölner Dreigestirn comprises Prinz, Bauer and Jungfrau; Dreigestirn also has broader uses elsewhere in German.

common.sentence: Beim Aufräumen nennt der Kollege die nutzlosen alten Kartons abfällig „Geraffel“.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted collective noun is an accusative naming complement with nennt; die nutzlosen alten Kartons is the accusative object being named.
language_specific.usage: The colloquial term dismisses the items as unwanted clutter.
language_specific.recognition: Bavarian and Austrian recognition: Geraffel is a regional colloquial term; Gerümpel is a de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Nach mehreren gescheiterten Anmeldeversuchen schimpft die Kollegin: „Was für ein Gfrett!“

language_specific.grammar: The noun appears in the exclamation was für ein Gfrett.
language_specific.usage: The colloquial exclamation expresses frustration at the troublesome registration attempts.
language_specific.recognition: Southern Germany and Austria recognition: Gfrett is a regional colloquial term; Ärger or Mühe can describe this sense in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im schwäbischen Gespräch kann „Gschmäckle“ einen verdächtigen Beigeschmack bezeichnen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of kann bezeichnen.
language_specific.usage: In this figurative use, the word hints that something may be improper without establishing wrongdoing.

common.sentence: In Österreich kann „Gspusi“ eine Liebesaffäre meinen.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Vertrag bezeichnet „Stockwerkeigentum“ Miteigentum mit Sonderrecht an einer Wohnung.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Grundbuch sichert ein „Schuldbrief“ eine Forderung durch ein Grundstück.

common.sentence: Das Schweizer Amt erhält ein „Betreibungsbegehren“ zur Eintreibung einer Forderung.

common.sentence: Das Schweizer „Spesenreglement“ regelt die Erstattung beruflicher Auslagen.

common.sentence: Das Schweizer „Arbeitsreglement“ enthält betriebliche Regeln für Beschäftigte.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht bezeichnet „Badi“ ein öffentliches Freibad.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Reisebericht bezeichnet „Beiz“ ein einfaches Gasthaus.

common.sentence: In Wien schimpft sie: „Mein Bruder ist ein Gfrast und hängt den ganzen Tag herum!“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular predicate noun after ist, referring to her brother.
language_specific.usage: The colloquial label is disparaging; she criticizes her brother's idleness.

common.sentence: In der Schweizer Meldung bedeutet „verzeigt“ hier bei der Polizei angezeigt.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted past participle identifies the result of reporting a person to an authority.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: verzeigen is Swiss Standard German; anzeigen is the usual de-DE equivalent in this context.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht werden die Vorschläge „vernehmlasst“, also zur öffentlichen Beratung vorgelegt.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted past participle forms a passive with werden; die Vorschläge are submitted for consultation.
language_specific.usage: The transitive verb is used in formal administrative contexts.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: vernehmlassen is Swiss Standard German; zur Beratung vorlegen is a descriptive de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: In Wien schimpft sie: „Der Wappler versucht zu helfen, aber er schafft wieder nichts!“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of versucht; er is the subject of schafft and refers to the same man.

common.sentence: In Wien nennt sie ihn ein „Tschapperl“, weil er ständig etwas umstößt.

common.sentence: In Österreich bezeichnet „Sachwalter“ historisch eine gerichtlich bestellte Vertretungsperson.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.

common.sentence: In Bayern nennt sie ihn einen „Hallodri“: Er vergisst ständig seine Zusagen.

common.sentence: In Österreich kann „Schmankerl“ eine besondere kulinarische Köstlichkeit bezeichnen.

common.sentence: In Österreich kann „Suderant“ eine Person bezeichnen, die ständig klagt.

common.sentence: In Berlin kann „Kodderschnauze“ eine Person mit vorlauter Ausdrucksweise bezeichnen.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of kann bezeichnen.

common.sentence: In Süddeutschland kann „Hock“ ein geselliges Treffen bezeichnen.

common.sentence: Vor den Gesprächen versuchten beide Delegationen, das Eis zu brechen.

language_specific.grammar: Das Eis is the accusative object of brechen. Das Eis brechen means to ease initial social tension.

common.sentence: Mit ihrer vorsichtigen Formulierung baute die Vermittlerin beiden Seiten eine Brücke.

language_specific.grammar: Eine Brücke is accusative; beiden Seiten is dative. The idiom means to make agreement or a change of position easier.

common.sentence: Nach der Beleidigung wollte der Botschafter kein Öl ins Feuer gießen.

language_specific.grammar: Öl is accusative; ins contracts in das and introduces accusative Feuer. The idiom means to aggravate a conflict. Feuer is neuter (das Feuer), plural Feuer.
language_specific.usage: The visible kein negates the idiom: the ambassador wants to avoid making the conflict worse.

common.sentence: Die Unterhändler ließen sich eine Hintertür offen, falls der Vertrag scheiterte.

language_specific.grammar: Eine Hintertür is accusative; sich is dative and refers to die Unterhändler. The idiom means to retain an alternative.

common.sentence: Mit der öffentlichen Drohung verbrannte der Minister alle Brücken zu seinen Partnern.

language_specific.grammar: Alle Brücken is accusative plural. Alle Brücken zu jemandem verbrennen means to destroy the possibility of restoring a relationship.

common.sentence: Die Sprecherin hielt sich bedeckt und verriet keine Einzelheiten des Angebots.

language_specific.grammar: Sich refers to die Sprecherin; bedeckt is a fixed predicate complement.
language_specific.usage: The idiom suggests deliberate reserve about information or intentions.

common.sentence: Die Delegation ließ durchblicken, dass sie zu weiteren Gesprächen bereit war.

language_specific.grammar: Durchblicken is an infinitive after ließ; the dass-clause gives the content hinted at. Durchblicken lassen means to hint at something; the visible lassen supplies the causative construction.
language_specific.pronunciation: Lemma durchblicken: [ˈdʊʁçˌblɪkən]; the stressed prefix is separable and the vowels are short.
language_specific.usage: The information is conveyed indirectly rather than announced plainly.

common.sentence: Beim Streit um die Grenze schlug die Vermittlerin ruhigere Töne an.

language_specific.grammar: Ruhigere Töne is accusative plural; an separates from schlug. The idiom describes adopting a less confrontational manner.

common.sentence: Trotz des Streits ließ die Ministerin den Gesprächsfaden nicht abreißen.

language_specific.grammar: Den Gesprächsfaden is the accusative object of abreißen lassen. The idiom describes allowing communication to lapse; nicht negates that outcome.

common.sentence: Der Minister forderte ein Verbot; mit ihrem Spott goss die Kritikerin Wasser auf seine Mühlen.

language_specific.grammar: Wasser is accusative; auf governs accusative seine Mühlen. Mühle is feminine (die Mühle), plural Mühlen; seine refers to the minister.
language_specific.usage: The idiom means that the critic's mockery strengthens the minister's position, whether or not she intended it.

common.sentence: Die Rezensentin nimmt kein Blatt vor den Mund: Der Roman sei langweilig.
common.lemma: kein Blatt vor den Mund nehmen
